insider_note: Both sides integrate to a log, so the answer combines back into a single log using log addition and log-power rules — that combination is what turns log y = log x² + log c into the clean power form y = cx².

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Divide by y and multiply by dx to put every y term with dy and every x term with dx.
steps.memory_tip: dy/y = 2dx/x is already fully separated — no further rearrangement needed before integrating.
steps.why: Dividing both sides by y and multiplying through by dx separates the variables immediately, since 2y/x·dx already carries the x and y factors on opposite sides once y is cleared.
common_mistakes: Cross-multiplying incorrectly and writing x dy = 2y dx instead of dy/y = 2dx/x.
Forgetting the factor of 2 when moving it across from the right side.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. ∫dy/y = log y and ∫2dx/x = 2 log x; combine the two logs and the constant into one power form.
steps.memory_tip: log y = log x² + log c combines to log y = log(cx²), so y = cx² — always write the constant as log c to combine logs cleanly.
lines: ∫dy/y = 2∫dx/x ⇒ log y = 2 log x + log c
⇒ log y = log x² + log c ⇒ log y = log(cx²)
steps.why: Writing the arbitrary constant as log c (instead of a bare c) lets every term combine into a single logarithm using log a + log b = log(ab) and n·log a = log(aⁿ); once both sides are a single log of the same base, the logs themselves can be dropped.
common_mistakes: Writing the constant of integration as +c instead of +log c, which prevents the logs from combining cleanly.
Stopping at log y = 2 log x + log c without finishing the simplification down to y = cx².
